title: Writing a circuit simulator from scratch
summary: How a netlist becomes a matrix, how a diode gets solved, and how a capacitor is stepped through time, in about 1,250 lines of C.
body:
## Goal

I use circuit simulators in class and on projects, but I treated them as a black box. I wanted to know what actually happens between typing a netlist and getting a waveform, so I wrote a small SPICE-style simulator in C with no libraries, and checked it against ngspice.

## How it works

**Every circuit becomes A x = b.** Kirchhoff's current law at each node gives one equation per node. The unknowns are the node voltages, plus one extra unknown for every voltage source and inductor, because their current can't be written from the voltages alone. Each element adds ("stamps") a few numbers into the matrix. A resistor between nodes a and b adds +1/R on the diagonal at a and b and −1/R off the diagonal. Solving the system gives every voltage at once.

**Capacitors become resistors, one step at a time.** A capacitor follows i = C dv/dt. Over one time step h, the trapezoid area rule from calculus turns that into a conductance 2C/h in parallel with a current source that carries the previous step's voltage and current. So at every time point the whole circuit is just resistors and sources again. This is the stamp in the code:

```
/* i_new = geq * v_new - ieq */
double geq = (pt->trap ? 2.0 : 1.0) * e->value / pt->h;
double ieq = geq * e->v_prev + (pt->trap ? e->i_prev : 0.0);
stamp_g(w, a, b, geq);
stamp_i(w, a, b, ieq);
```

**Diodes need Newton-Raphson.** The diode current is exponential in voltage, so the system isn't linear any more. The fix is to replace the diode with its tangent line at the current guess, solve, re-linearize at the new answer, and repeat until the answer stops moving.

![tinyspice waveforms overlaid on exact solutions and ngspice for four circuits](/assets/figures/tiny-spice/validation.png "Fig. 1 · tinyspice vs exact solutions and ngspice. The buck converter matches ngspice to 0.009 % RMS.")

## What needed extra care

Getting the basic loop right was the easy part. Making it robust took most of the work, and every fix turned out to be something real SPICE also does:

- **Ringing at sharp edges.** The trapezoidal rule oscillates right after a discontinuity, like the edge of a PULSE source. One backward-Euler step after each corner damps it.
- **Exponential overflow.** A bad Newton guess can push the diode voltage high enough that e<sup>V/nVt</sup> overflows. Junction-voltage limiting caps how far one iteration can move.
- **Missing corners.** If a time step jumps over the corner of a pulse, the waveform is wrong. Breakpoints make the stepper land exactly on every corner.
- **No DC starting point.** When Newton can't find the operating point, gmin stepping starts with large conductances to ground (an easy, nearly linear problem) and removes them gradually.

> **Note:** Halving the time step cut the error by 4× with the trapezoidal rule and by 2× with backward Euler. The measured slopes were 1.92 and 0.98, matching the theory (error ∝ h² vs h).

## Next

A MOSFET model, AC small-signal analysis, and a sparse solver so it can handle thousands of nodes instead of hundreds. The code is on [GitHub](https://github.com/radhepa/tinyspice).

title: SiC Inverter 800, part 1: a MOSFET model from the datasheet
summary: Before any design decision, I needed a simulation model of the silicon-carbide MOSFET that reproduces its datasheet. Here is how I built and checked it.
body:
## Goal

The project is one switch of an 800 V electric-vehicle traction inverter. Every later choice (gate resistors, how many devices in parallel, switching frequency) depends on simulated switching losses, and those are only as good as the transistor model. Manufacturers publish curves, not equations, so the first job was a SPICE model of the Wolfspeed C3M0021120K (1200 V, 21 mΩ) that matches its datasheet.

## How it works

The model is an equivalent circuit, and each piece is fitted to a different datasheet figure:

- **Channel current**: a square-law MOSFET with a smooth turn-on, fitted to the transfer curve.
- **Drift resistance** that grows with temperature, R ∝ T<sup>2.34</sup>, because electron mobility in SiC falls as it heats up. Fitted to R<sub>DS(on)</sub> vs temperature.
- **Capacitances** C<sub>gs</sub>, C<sub>gd</sub>(V) and C<sub>ds</sub>(V), fitted to the capacitance curves, the output-capacitance energy and the gate-charge curve.
- **Body diode**: a PiN diode with a ~3 V knee, fitted to the V<sub>SD</sub> curves and reverse-recovery charge.

Then a **double-pulse test**, the standard way industry measures switching loss, was built around it in ngspice. Five unknowns about the datasheet's test fixture (driver resistance, edge time, loop inductance, inductor capacitance, diode lifetime) were fitted at a single operating point.

![Fitted MOSFET model curves overlaid on datasheet curves](/assets/figures/sic-inverter-800/01_device_fit.png "Fig. 1 · Model vs datasheet. R<sub>DS(on)</sub> 20.2 / 35.1 mΩ at 25 / 175 °C (datasheet 21 / 36), gate charge 162 nC (162).")

## What went wrong

The first model switched about 30 % too fast. Checking its internals showed why: the datasheet's gate-charge curve puts the Miller plateau at 6.3 V (20 A, 800 V), while the transfer curve predicts 5.2 V. I added a threshold shift that grows with V<sub>DS</sub>, fitted to that one point.

With that fix, the fitted thresholds came out at 2.53 V and 1.98 V. The datasheet specifies 2.5 V and 2.0 V, and those numbers were never used in the fit. That is good independent evidence the model is physically right, not just curve-matched.

> **Validation:** On 13 operating points not used in calibration, switching energy error was 3.6 % on average across current and 1.8 % across temperature. The model under-predicts how much a large gate resistor slows switching (up to 24 % at 20 Ω), so the later Monte Carlo adds a 10 % energy uncertainty to cover it.

## Next

Using the calibrated bench to pick gate resistors, set a layout-inductance budget, and decide on negative gate bias and a Miller clamp. The full design is in the [case study](/projects/sic-inverter-800/).

title: Li-ion BMS, part 1: design overview
summary: A battery management system for a 4-cell pack, from public lab data to C firmware: what each piece does and how they connect.
body:
## Goal

Build the brain of a small battery pack: four LG HG2 18650 cells in series (16.8 V). It has to keep the pack safe, estimate how much charge is left, and keep the cells balanced, and I wanted every number to be checked against real measurements rather than made up.

## How it works

The project starts from public lab data for this exact cell (McMaster University, CC BY 4.0) and moves toward firmware in five steps:

1. **Cell model.** A slow C/20 test gives the open-circuit voltage curve. A pulse test (HPPC) gives a resistance and two RC pairs at each state of charge. Together they predict the cell's voltage for any current.
2. **Validation.** The model is run on four EPA drive cycles it was never fitted to. Voltage error: 14.5 to 23.7 mV RMS.
3. **State of charge.** An Extended Kalman Filter runs the model alongside the real cell and uses the voltage difference to correct its SOC estimate.
4. **Firmware.** Protection, the EKF and balancing in hardware-independent C99, with the model tables generated straight from the Python code.
5. **Testing.** Unit tests, then software-in-the-loop runs on recorded lab data with faults injected.

![State of charge on a UDDS drive cycle: EKF, Coulomb counting and true value](/assets/figures/li-ion-bms/04_soc_udds.png "Fig. 1 · Starting 50 % wrong with a 50 mA sensor offset, the EKF converges within seconds; Coulomb counting with a perfect start still drifts.")

## What went wrong

Two things in the cell model needed fixing after validation:

- Below about 20 % SOC, the RC fits ran into their parameter limits and gave nonsense. Those fits are dropped and the last good values are held.
- I first used the average of the charge and discharge OCV curves. A drive cycle mostly discharges, so it sits on the discharge side of the hysteresis loop. Switching to the discharge-side curve halved the drive-cycle error.

Testing also found a system-level problem: in city driving, regenerative braking pulses reach 5.3 A, above the cell's 4.5 A charge limit, so the firmware would open the charge FET. That isn't a firmware bug; the vehicle has to cap regen at the BMS limit, and I wrote it down as a requirement.

> **Note:** Mid-SOC, a 1 % change in charge moves the cell voltage only 6–10 mV. That is why a Kalman filter beats simple voltage lookup: it has to weigh a small, noisy voltage signal against current integration.

## Next

A closer look at the EKF and how it was tuned, then temperature-dependent parameters. The full project is in the [case study](/projects/li-ion-bms/).
